title: Networking: Devices, Topologies & Protocols
summary: Network types and topologies, devices (hub/switch/router), the OSI model, IP addressing and TCP/UDP with port numbers. Device-to-layer matching and IP-class identification are CKT regulars.

subtopics.title: Network types and topologies
subtopics.concept: Networks are named by how far they reach: PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN, from small to large. A topology is the shape of the wiring: bus, ring, star, mesh, tree or hybrid. Star is the shape used in modern offices. A full mesh of n computers needs n(n-1)/2 links.

tricks.title: Mesh half-row sum
tricks.body: Full-mesh links for n nodes are n(n-1)/2. Compute it each time. Do not memorise per-n values.

example.q: How many links does a full mesh of 8 computers need?
steps: Each computer has 7 links.
8 x 7 = 56, and each link is counted twice.

tricks.title: PLMW span ladder
tricks.body: PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN: Personal, Local, Metropolitan, Wide. The Internet is the largest WAN.

example.q: A network limited to one office building is a?
steps: One building is a local span.
Local Area Network.

tricks.title: Star means central device
tricks.body: If the question says the central device fails and the whole network stops, it describes star topology.

example.q: In which topology is the central hub a single point of failure?
steps: Every node hangs off the hub.
If the hub fails, none can talk.

mistakes.wrong: Using the bus topology's weakness (backbone break) for star questions.
mistakes.right: Star fails at the central hub or switch. Bus fails at the backbone.

mistakes.wrong: Counting mesh links as $n^2$.
mistakes.right: Use n(n-1)/2. Each link is counted once, not twice.

mistakes.wrong: Calling Wi-Fi IEEE 802.3.
mistakes.right: 802.3 is wired Ethernet. Wi-Fi is 802.11.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Internet a MAN or a LAN.
mistakes.right: The Internet is the largest WAN.

subtopics.notes:
### Networks by their reach
Name a network by how far it stretches. The order is PAN, then LAN, then MAN, then WAN.

| Type | Span | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|
| **PAN** (Personal Area Network) | about 10 metres around one person | Bluetooth headset with a phone |
| **LAN** (Local Area Network) | one building or campus | school computer lab, office floor |
| **MAN** (Metropolitan Area Network) | one city | city cable network |
| **WAN** (Wide Area Network) | countries or continents | the **Internet is the largest WAN** |

A LAN is privately owned and fast. A WAN uses leased lines over long distances.

> **Tip:** Match the span in the question, not the technology. "One office building" is always a LAN.

### Topologies, the shape of the wiring
A **topology** is the way computers are laid out and joined. Learn the table row by row.

| Topology | Layout | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bus** | all nodes tap one backbone cable with terminators | cheapest | backbone break kills all; collisions |
| **Ring** | each node joins exactly two neighbours | orderly token passing | one break can halt the loop |
| **Star** | every node joins a central hub or switch | one cable failure hurts one node only | the central device is a single point of failure |
| **Mesh** | every node joins every other node | most reliable | most cables, costliest |
| **Tree** | hierarchy of stars joined on a bus | scales to large LANs | root failure splits the tree |
| **Hybrid** | a mix of the above | fits real networks | more complex |

> **Rule:** Star is the most common shape today. Mesh is the most reliable.

### Counting mesh links
In a full mesh of n computers, each one has n - 1 links. Every link is counted twice that way, so halve the total.

$$\text{links}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$$

> **Example:** For 6 computers, $6\times5\div2=15$ links. For 8 computers, $8\times7\div2=28$ links.

Never use $n^2$. Check small cases: 4 computers give 6 links, 5 give 10.

### Client-server, peer-to-peer and VPN
- **Client-server:** dedicated servers serve many client machines.
- **Peer-to-peer:** all machines are equals. Each can share and use resources.
- **VPN:** builds an encrypted private tunnel over a public network.

### Wireless and IEEE standards
- **Ethernet** (wired LAN) is IEEE **802.3**.
- **Wi-Fi** (wireless LAN) is IEEE **802.11**. The versions n, ac and ax are called Wi-Fi 4, 5 and 6.
- **Bluetooth** is IEEE **802.15**. It is a PAN of about 10 metres.
- **Infrared** needs a clear line of sight.

> **Watch:** Wi-Fi is not 802.3. The number 802.3 belongs to wired Ethernet.

patterns.name: Network type by span
patterns.howToSpot: A situation is described (school lab, city cable, worldwide web, one person's Bluetooth) and PAN, LAN, MAN or WAN is asked.
steps: Line up the ladder: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN.
Find the span in the question: person, building, city or world.
Pick the type with that span.
Remember the Internet is the largest WAN.
patterns.why: The span, not the technology, names the network.

example.q: A computer lab of one school connected by a switch forms a
steps: The lab is inside one building.
One building means a local span.

patterns.name: Topology identification by description
patterns.howToSpot: The layout is described (all nodes to a central device, every node to every other, one backbone, a circle) and the topology is asked.
steps: Central device with all nodes on it: Star.
Every node linked to every other: Mesh.
One shared backbone cable with terminators: Bus.
Closed circle of neighbours: Ring. Stars joined on a backbone: Tree.
patterns.why: Each topology has one giveaway layout phrase.

example.q: In which topology is every computer connected to a central hub or switch?
steps: Central hub or switch is the giveaway.
One cable break isolates only one node.

patterns.name: Mesh link count (numeric)
patterns.howToSpot: How many links are needed for a full mesh of n computers? It is pure arithmetic.
steps: Write the formula n(n-1)/2.
Put in n and multiply n by n - 1.
Halve the product.
Check with n = 4 giving 6.
patterns.why: Each line is counted twice if you multiply n by n - 1.

example.q: How many cable links are needed for a full mesh of 6 computers?

patterns.name: Topology strengths and failure points
patterns.howToSpot: A statement says which topology is cheapest, most reliable, has a single point of failure, or what happens when a cable breaks.
steps: Star: one cable break hurts one node. Hub failure stops all.
Bus: backbone break means total failure. It is the cheapest.
Mesh: most reliable, most cable, costliest.
Ring: one broken node or link can stop the ring.
patterns.why: The weakness of each shape follows from how it is wired.

example.q: In a star topology, failure of the central hub results in
steps: Every node depends on the hub.
Individual cables do not matter here.

patterns.name: IEEE standards and LAN jargon
patterns.howToSpot: Wi-Fi is IEEE what, or Ethernet works on which standard. It is matching 802.x numbers to technologies.
steps: Ethernet (wired) is 802.3.
Wi-Fi (wireless) is 802.11.
Bluetooth is 802.15.
Watch for the trap of pairing Wi-Fi with 802.3.
patterns.why: The 802 family names the wire or the air.

example.q: Wi-Fi networks are standardised under IEEE
steps: Wi-Fi is wireless LAN.
802.3 is wired, 802.15 is Bluetooth.

patterns.name: Network models, VPN and wireless links
patterns.howToSpot: Questions ask what a VPN does, how client-server differs from peer-to-peer, or the range of Bluetooth.
steps: VPN: an encrypted private tunnel over a public network.
Client-server: dedicated servers serve clients.
Peer-to-peer: all machines are equals.
Bluetooth is a PAN of about 10 m. Infrared needs line of sight.
patterns.why: Each term has one short definition to recall.

example.q: Which technology builds an encrypted private tunnel over a public network?
steps: The key words are encrypted and private tunnel.
Public network means the Internet.

revision: PAN (10 m) < LAN (building) < MAN (city) < WAN (country or world).
The Internet is the largest WAN.
Bus = one backbone. Ring = circle of neighbours. Star = central hub or switch. Mesh = all to all.
Full-mesh links = n(n-1)/2. Six computers give 15 links.
Star's weakness is the central device. Bus's weakness is the backbone.
Ethernet is 802.3, Wi-Fi is 802.11, Bluetooth is 802.15.

subtopics.title: Network devices
subtopics.concept: Each network device has one job. A hub broadcasts to all ports. A switch sends to the right port by MAC address. A router joins different networks by IP address. A modem converts digital and analog signals. Exams rarely name the device. They describe its job.

tricks.title: Hub, switch, router ladder
tricks.body: Hub hears and shouts to all (layer 1). Switch is selective, by MAC (layer 2). Router routes between networks by IP (layer 3). 'Broadcasts to all' means hub. 'MAC address table' means switch. 'Connects two different networks' means router.

example.q: Which device forwards data only to the intended port using MAC addresses?
steps: Selective forwarding is the switch's job.
The MAC table decides the port.

tricks.title: Modem is modulator plus demodulator
tricks.body: The full form is the answer. Digital data is modulated onto an analog carrier and demodulated back. 'Digital to analog conversion' in a question means modem.

example.q: Which device converts digital signals to analog and back?
steps: Modulate means digital to analog.
Demodulate means analog to digital.

mistakes.wrong: Saying a hub forwards data selectively.
mistakes.right: That is the switch. A hub always broadcasts to every port.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the router at the Data Link layer.
mistakes.right: A router reads IP addresses, so it sits at the Network layer (3).

mistakes.wrong: Confusing a gateway with a router.
mistakes.right: A gateway converts protocols. A router selects routes.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking the MAC address changes with the network.
mistakes.right: MAC is permanent and physical. The IP is the one that is assigned.

subtopics.notes:
### The device ladder
Learn each device with its layer and its one job.

| Device | Layer | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Repeater** | Physical (1) | regenerates a weak signal to extend range |
| **Hub** | Physical (1) | broadcasts every bit to every port; no intelligence |
| **Bridge** | Data Link (2) | joins two LAN segments and filters by MAC |
| **Switch** | Data Link (2) | learns MAC addresses and sends frames only to the right port |
| **NIC** | Data Link (2) | connects one machine to the network; carries its MAC |
| **Access Point** | Data Link (2) | puts Wi-Fi devices onto the wired LAN |
| **Router** | Network (3) | joins different networks and picks routes by IP |
| **Gateway** | up to Application (7) | converts between different protocol systems |

> **Tip:** Hub is a dumb loudspeaker. Switch is a smart postman. Router is the link between cities.

### Modem and firewall
A **modem** is a MOdulator-DEModulator. It turns the PC's digital data into analog signals for a phone or cable line. It turns analog back to digital.

A **firewall** is a rule filter in hardware or software. It allows or blocks traffic by rule. It can work at several layers.

### The one-line differences
- **Hub vs switch:** a hub shouts to everyone. A switch sends only to the destination port. It is faster and safer.
- **Switch vs router:** a switch moves data inside one network by MAC. A router moves data between networks by IP.
- **Repeater vs amplifier:** a repeater regenerates a clean digital signal. An amplifier boosts the noise too.
- **Gateway vs router:** a router chooses routes. A gateway translates between protocol worlds.

> **Note:** Your home router joins your LAN to the Internet.

### MAC address, the burnt-in identity
Every NIC carries a **48-bit physical address**, for example 1A:2B:3C:4D:5E:6F. The maker fixes it.

- **MAC:** physical and permanent. Switches read it.
- **IP:** logical and assigned. Routers read it.

### A home network in four steps
Follow one message from a laptop to a website. This shows where each device sits.

1. The laptop's **NIC** puts the data on the network. It carries the laptop's MAC address.
2. An **access point** takes the Wi-Fi signal and passes it to the wired LAN.
3. A **switch** sends the frames to the router's port only, using its MAC table.
4. The **router** reads the IP address and forwards the packets to the Internet.

A **modem** sits between the router and the phone or cable line. It converts digital and analog signals.

### Reading a device question
Find the verb first. Then name the device.

| Job in the question | Device |
|---|---|
| sends to all ports | hub |
| sends only to the destination port | switch |
| connects two different networks, chooses a path | router |
| regenerates a weak signal | repeater |
| converts protocols | gateway |
| digital to analog and back | modem |

> **Watch:** When a layer is asked, use the ladder. No address is layer 1. MAC is layer 2. IP is layer 3.

patterns.name: Hub vs switch vs router
patterns.howToSpot: A behaviour is described (sends to all ports, forwards to the right port, connects two networks and picks a path) and the device is asked.
steps: Sends to all ports: hub (layer 1).
Sends to the right port by MAC: switch (layer 2).
Joins different networks by IP: router (layer 3).
More intelligent than a hub: switch.
patterns.why: The job words point to exactly one device.

example.q: Which device forwards data only to the intended port instead of all ports?
steps: Forwarding to one port needs a MAC table.
Hubs broadcast to every port.

patterns.name: Modem, repeater, bridge, gateway functions
patterns.howToSpot: A modem is used for, a device that regenerates a weak signal, or a device that converts between protocols. It is function-to-device matching.
steps: Modem: digital signal to analog and back.
Repeater: regenerates weak signals.
Bridge: joins two LAN segments.
Gateway: translates between protocol systems.
patterns.why: Each device is named after its single job.

example.q: The device that regenerates and retransmits a weakening signal is a
steps: Regenerating a signal is the repeater's job.
It restores the clean signal so the cable can run farther.

patterns.name: Device-to-layer matching
patterns.howToSpot: A router works on which OSI layer, or a hub operates at layer what. It is a device and layer pair.
steps: Hub and repeater: layer 1 (Physical).
Switch, bridge and NIC: layer 2 (Data Link).
Router: layer 3 (Network).
Gateway reaches up to the Application layer.
patterns.why: The address type a device reads fixes its layer.

example.q: A router operates on which layer of the OSI model?
steps: A router uses IP addresses.
IP addresses belong to layer 3, the Network layer.

patterns.name: NIC and MAC-address facts
patterns.howToSpot: A MAC address is how many bits, where it is stored, or how MAC differs from IP.
steps: MAC is a 48-bit physical address.
The maker burns it into the NIC.
MAC is permanent. IP is assigned and changes.
Switches use MAC. Routers use IP.
patterns.why: MAC identifies the card. IP identifies the place in a network.

example.q: The physical address burnt into a network interface card is the
steps: A burnt-in, factory-fixed address is physical.
The IP is only a logical label.

patterns.name: Firewall and access point
patterns.howToSpot: A device that allows or blocks traffic by rules, or a device that lets Wi-Fi devices join a wired LAN.
steps: Allows or blocks traffic by rules: firewall.
Joins wireless clients to a wired LAN: access point.
A firewall can be hardware or software.
An access point works at layer 2.
patterns.why: Both devices guard or open a door to the network.

example.q: Which device filters traffic by rules to allow or block it?
steps: Rule-based allow or block is filtering.
That is a firewall.

patterns.name: One-line device differences
patterns.howToSpot: Statements compare two devices: switch vs router, repeater vs amplifier, gateway vs router.
steps: Switch: inside one network, by MAC. Router: between networks, by IP.
Repeater regenerates a clean signal. An amplifier also boosts noise.
Router selects routes. Gateway translates protocols.
Pick the option that matches the job.
patterns.why: Each pair differs in one key job.

example.q: Which device translates between different protocol systems?
steps: A router only chooses routes.
Protocol translation is the gateway's job.

revision: Hub broadcasts (layer 1). Switch learns MAC and sends to the right port (layer 2). Router routes between networks by IP (layer 3).
Repeater regenerates a signal (layer 1). Bridge joins two LANs (layer 2).
Gateway is a protocol converter.
Modem is a modulator plus a demodulator (digital to analog and back).
NIC carries the 48-bit MAC address.
MAC is permanent and physical. IP is logical and assigned.

subtopics.title: OSI and TCP/IP reference models
subtopics.concept: The OSI model splits network work into 7 layers, so each layer can be built and replaced on its own. The TCP/IP model has 4 layers, and the real Internet runs on it. Most exam questions ask the layer count, the order, or which layer does a given job.

tricks.title: OSI mnemonics
tricks.body: Bottom-up: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application). Top-down: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

example.q: Which OSI layer comes directly above the Network layer?
steps: Bottom-up order: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport.
Transport follows Network.

tricks.title: Layer-device pairs
tricks.body: Router is layer 3. Switch and bridge are layer 2. Hub and repeater are layer 1. Use the address type: IP is 3, MAC is 2, no address is 1.

example.q: At which OSI layer does a router operate?
steps: A router reads IP addresses.
IP belongs to the Network layer.

mistakes.wrong: Counting 4 or 5 OSI layers.
mistakes.right: OSI has 7 layers. TCP/IP has 4.

mistakes.wrong: Putting encryption at the Application layer.
mistakes.right: Encryption, formatting and compression sit in Presentation (6).

mistakes.wrong: Saying the Session layer routes packets.
mistakes.right: Routing is the Network layer (3). Session manages dialogues.

mistakes.wrong: Placing TCP and UDP at the Network layer.
mistakes.right: TCP and UDP are Transport layer (4). IP is Network layer (3).

subtopics.notes:
### Why a reference model exists
Sending data needs many jobs: signals, framing, addressing, delivery, dialogue control, translation and user services. The **OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model** splits them into **7 layers**. Each layer can be designed and replaced on its own.

### The 7 layers, bottom to top

| # | Layer | Job | Works with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Physical** | raw **bits** on the medium | cables, hubs, repeaters |
| 2 | **Data Link** | **frames**, MAC addresses, error detection | Ethernet, switches, bridges, NIC |
| 3 | **Network** | logical addressing and **routing** | IP, routers |
| 4 | **Transport** | end-to-end delivery, ports, reliability | TCP, UDP |
| 5 | **Session** | opens, manages and closes dialogues | NetBIOS, RPC |
| 6 | **Presentation** | format, **encryption**, compression | JPEG, MP3, SSL/TLS |
| 7 | **Application** | user-facing network services | HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS |

> **Tip:** Bottom-up: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away". Top-down: "All People Seem To Need Data Processing".

### Data units on the way down
Data changes name at each layer as it moves down the sender's stack.

- Layer 4 makes **segments**.
- Layer 3 makes **packets**.
- Layer 2 makes **frames**.
- Layer 1 sends **bits**.

The receiver does the reverse, from layer 1 up to layer 7.

### How layer questions are asked
- **Device to layer:** hub and repeater are layer 1. Switch and bridge are layer 2. Router is layer 3.
- **Job to layer:** routing is Network (3). Framing and MAC are Data Link (2). Encryption and compression are Presentation (6).
- **Number:** OSI has 7 layers. TCP/IP has 4.

> **Watch:** Encryption is not Application. Routing is not Transport. Test the planted option against its neighbour layer.

### Sorting a layer question
First decide what the question really asks. Then use the matching tool.

| Question asks | What to do |
|---|---|
| a **number** | 7 for OSI, 4 for TCP/IP |
| an **order** | use the mnemonic and count |
| a **job** | match the job to one layer |
| a **worker** (device or protocol) | use the address type or the job |

> **Example:** "Which layer delivers data end to end using ports?" The job is end-to-end delivery. That is Transport (4).

For job questions, compare the planted option with its neighbour. Transport only delivers after the Network layer has found the path. Application serves the user. Presentation prepares the data format for it.

### The TCP/IP model
The real Internet runs on TCP/IP. OSI is the teaching map.

| TCP/IP layer | OSI layers it covers |
|---|---|
| **Application** | 5 + 6 + 7 (Session, Presentation, Application) |
| **Transport** | 4 |
| **Internet** | 3 (Network) |
| **Network Access / Link** | 1 + 2 (Physical, Data Link) |

> **Rule:** Which model has 4 layers? TCP/IP.

patterns.name: OSI layer count and order
patterns.howToSpot: How many layers does the OSI model have, an ordering question, or the layer directly above or below another.
steps: Recall the 7 layers from Physical (1) to Application (7).
Use a mnemonic to fix the order.
Transport is the 4th, the middle layer.
Count up or down from the layer given.
patterns.why: The order never changes, so a mnemonic is enough.

example.q: How many layers are there in the OSI reference model?
steps: OSI is the 7-layer model.
The 4-layer model is TCP/IP.

patterns.name: Function-to-layer matching
patterns.howToSpot: Routing is done at which layer, encryption or compression is a which-layer function, or framing and MAC addressing belong to which layer.
steps: Bits on cables: Physical (1).
Frames and MAC: Data Link (2). Routing: Network (3).
Delivery and ports: Transport (4). Dialogues: Session (5).
Encryption and compression: Presentation (6). User services: Application (7).
patterns.why: Each layer owns one clear job.

example.q: Encryption and data compression are functions of which OSI layer?
steps: Data format work sits below the Application.
That layer is Presentation.

patterns.name: Device and protocol-to-layer matching
patterns.howToSpot: A switch works at which layer, HTTP is a which-layer protocol, or TCP sits in which layer.
steps: Hub and repeater are layer 1; switch and bridge layer 2; router layer 3.
TCP and UDP are layer 4.
HTTP, FTP and SMTP are layer 7. IP is layer 3.
Match the job before the name.
patterns.why: A device or protocol lives at the layer of its job.

example.q: TCP and UDP work at which layer of the OSI model?
steps: They deliver data end to end.
They use port numbers.

patterns.name: TCP/IP model vs OSI
patterns.howToSpot: The TCP/IP model has how many layers, which OSI layers merge into TCP/IP Application, or mapping the four TCP/IP layers.
steps: TCP/IP has 4 layers.
Network Access covers OSI 1 and 2. Internet is 3.
Transport is 4.
Application covers OSI 5, 6 and 7.
patterns.why: TCP/IP merges the top three and bottom two OSI layers.

example.q: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have?
steps: Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.
That makes four.

patterns.name: Data unit at each layer
patterns.howToSpot: What is the data unit at layer 2, or data is called packets at which layer.
steps: Layer 4: segments.
Layer 3: packets.
Layer 2: frames. Layer 1: bits.
Data moves down the sender and up the receiver.
patterns.why: Each layer wraps data and gives it a new name.

example.q: Data is called a frame at which OSI layer?
steps: Frames carry MAC addresses.
MAC belongs to Data Link.

revision: OSI has 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
Router is layer 3, switch is layer 2, hub is layer 1.
Routing is Network. Encryption and compression are Presentation.
Transport layer holds TCP and UDP and uses ports. Session manages dialogues.
Data units: segments (4), packets (3), frames (2), bits (1).
TCP/IP has 4 layers: Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.

subtopics.title: IP addressing: IPv4 classes and IPv6
subtopics.concept: An IPv4 address has 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255. The first number decides the class. IPv6 has 128 bits, written in hexadecimal with colons. 127.0.0.1 is loopback, and 192.168.x.x is a private range.

tricks.title: Class ruler
tricks.body: Remember the cut-points 1, 128, 192, 224, 240. A starts at 1, B at 128, C at 192, D (multicast) at 224, E at 240. The number 127 is loopback, between A and B.

example.q: What is the class of 172.16.0.1?
steps: Read only the first octet: 172.
172 lies in 128 to 191.

tricks.title: Loopback is 127
tricks.body: 127.0.0.1 is localhost. Pinging it tests your own TCP/IP stack, not the cable. Any question with 127.x wants loopback.

example.q: Pinging 127.0.0.1 tests what?
steps: 127.0.0.1 is the machine itself.
It never leaves the computer.
example.answer: The local machine's own TCP/IP setup

tricks.title: IPv4 vs IPv6 size
tricks.body: IPv4 is 32 bits in dotted decimal. IPv6 is 128 bits in colon-separated hexadecimal. If addresses are running out, IPv6 is the fix.

example.q: How many bits does an IPv6 address have?
steps: IPv4 has 32 bits.
IPv6 has 128 bits.

mistakes.wrong: Calling 127.0.0.1 a Class A host address.
mistakes.right: 127 is reserved for loopback. Class A networks end at 126.

mistakes.wrong: Calling 192.168.1.1 a public address.
mistakes.right: It is the classic private home-router address.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing the MAC address with the IP address.
mistakes.right: MAC is 48-bit, physical and burnt in. IP is logical and assigned.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the whole address to find the class.
mistakes.right: Only the first octet decides the class.

mistakes.wrong: Giving all 256 addresses of Class C as usable hosts.
mistakes.right: Two are reserved, so 254 are usable.

subtopics.notes:
### IPv4, the 32-bit address
An **IPv4 address** has **32 bits**. It is written as four numbers from 0 to 255 with dots, like 192.168.1.1. Each number is an **octet** (8 bits). The first octet decides the class.

| Class | First octet | Default mask | Hosts per network | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 1 - 126 | 255.0.0.0 (/8) | 1,67,77,214 | huge networks |
| **B** | 128 - 191 | 255.255.0.0 (/16) | 65,534 | large organisations |
| **C** | 192 - 223 | 255.255.255.0 (/24) | 254 | small networks |
| **D** | 224 - 239 | none | none | multicasting |
| **E** | 240 - 255 | none | none | experimental or research |

> **Tip:** Anchor the ruler at 1, 128, 192, 224 and 240. Drop the given number between them.

### Usable hosts
Two addresses in each network are reserved: the network address and the broadcast address.

> **Example:** Class C has 256 addresses. Take away 2. That leaves **254 usable hosts**.

### Special addresses
- **127.0.0.1** is loopback or localhost. A machine talks to itself. Pinging it tests your own TCP/IP stack.
- **0.0.0.0** is the unspecified address.
- **255.255.255.255** is the broadcast address.
- **Private ranges** are not routed on the Internet: 10.0.0.0/8, 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, and 192.168.0.0/16.

> **Watch:** 127 is not a Class A network. Class A ends at 126. Home routers use 192.168.x.x, which is private.

### IPv6, the 128-bit address
IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses. That is too few for the connected world. **IPv6 uses 128 bits**. It is written as **eight groups of hexadecimal digits** with colons, for example 2001:0db8::7334. A double colon can shorten a run of zeros.

### MAC and IP compared

| | MAC address | IP address |
|---|---|---|
| Type | physical, burnt into the NIC | logical, assigned |
| Size | 48 bits | IPv4 32 bits, IPv6 128 bits |
| Changes | never | changes with the network |
| Used by | switches (layer 2) | routers (layer 3) |

**DHCP** gives IP addresses automatically. A **static** address is set by hand.

### Worked class checks
Cover everything after the first dot. Look at the first octet only.

| Address | First octet | Class |
|---|---|---|
| 10.0.0.5 | 10 | A |
| 130.10.5.2 | 130 | B |
| 196.1.2.3 | 196 | C |
| 225.5.4.1 | 225 | D (multicast) |
| 245.0.0.1 | 245 | E |

> **Rule:** 127.x.x.x is never a Class A host address. It is loopback.

### Checking a private address
A private address starts with 10, or with 172 and a second number from 16 to 31, or with 192.168. A 172 address with second number 32 or more is public.

patterns.name: IP class identification
patterns.howToSpot: An address is given (10.0.0.5, 130.10.5.2, 196.1.2.3, 225.5.4.1) and its class is asked, or the range of a class is asked.
steps: Read only the first octet.
224-239 is D (multicast). 240-255 is E.
Treat 127 as loopback, not Class A.
patterns.why: The first octet alone fixes the class.

example.q: The IP address 196.20.5.1 belongs to which class?
steps: The first octet is 196.
196 lies between 192 and 223.

patterns.name: Private ranges and loopback
patterns.howToSpot: Which is a private IP address, what is 127.0.0.1, or which address is reserved for testing or localhost.
steps: Home routers use 192.168.x.x.
127.0.0.1 is loopback (localhost).
169.254.x.x appears when automatic addressing fails (APIPA).
patterns.why: Private and loopback ranges are reserved and never routed on the Internet.

example.q: The address 127.0.0.1 is used for
steps: 127 is the reserved loopback block.
The computer talks to itself.

patterns.name: IPv4 vs IPv6 facts
patterns.howToSpot: IPv4 has how many bits, IPv6 is written in what form, how many groups in an IPv6 address, or why IPv6 was needed.
steps: IPv4: 32 bits, four decimal octets, about 4.3 billion addresses.
IPv6: 128 bits, eight hexadecimal groups with colons.
IPv6 was needed because IPv4 addresses ran out.
patterns.why: More bits mean a far larger address space.

example.q: An IPv6 address is how many bits long?
steps: IPv6 has eight groups.
Eight groups of 16 bits make 128 bits.

patterns.name: MAC vs IP and usable-host counts
patterns.howToSpot: Difference between MAC and IP, how many hosts a Class C network can have, or which address changes when you move networks.
steps: MAC: 48-bit, physical, permanent.
IP: logical, assigned, changes with the network.
Class C: 256 - 2 = 254 usable hosts.
patterns.why: Two addresses in every network are reserved.

example.q: How many usable host addresses does a Class C network provide?
steps: Class C has 256 addresses.
Take away the network and broadcast addresses: 254.

patterns.name: Default masks and special addresses
patterns.howToSpot: The default mask of a class, the broadcast address, or the unspecified address.
steps: 0.0.0.0 is unspecified.
255.255.255.255 is the broadcast address.
patterns.why: The mask shows how many leading bits name the network.

example.q: What is the default subnet mask of a Class B network?
steps: Class B has a /16 prefix.
Two full octets of 255.

patterns.name: DHCP and static addressing
patterns.howToSpot: Which protocol assigns IP addresses automatically, or how static addressing differs from it.
steps: DHCP gives IP addresses automatically.
Static addressing sets them by hand.
DHCP uses ports 67 and 68.
patterns.why: Automatic assignment saves manual setup.

example.q: Which protocol assigns IP addresses automatically to devices?
steps: Automatic assignment is the job of DHCP.
Its full form is Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol.

revision: IPv4 has 32 bits in four octets from 0 to 255. IPv6 has 128 bits in hexadecimal with colons.
127.0.0.1 is loopback.
A Class C network has 254 usable hosts.
MAC is 48-bit and physical. IP is logical.
DHCP gives IP addresses automatically.

subtopics.title: Protocols and port numbers; TCP vs UDP
subtopics.concept: The IP address finds the computer. The port number finds the service on it. Learn the main ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, POP3 110, IMAP 143. TCP is reliable and connection-oriented. UDP is fast and connectionless.

tricks.title: Port anchors
tricks.body: Memorise six first: 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 110 POP3, 21 FTP. Then 22 SSH and 23 Telnet. Telnet is the insecure one.

example.q: What is the default port of HTTPS?
steps: HTTPS is the secure web protocol.
Its port is 443.

tricks.title: TCP tracks, UDP does not
tricks.body: TCP tracks every packet, so it is reliable but slower. UDP is unreliable but quick. 'Guaranteed delivery' in a question means TCP.

example.q: Live cricket video streaming mainly uses which protocol?
steps: Speed matters more than perfect delivery.
Retransmission would pause the match.

mistakes.wrong: Giving HTTP the port 443.
mistakes.right: 443 is HTTPS. Plain HTTP is 80.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing TCP for live streaming.
mistakes.right: The expected answer is UDP, because speed comes first.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Telnet is secure.
mistakes.right: SSH (22) is encrypted. Telnet (23) sends plain text.

mistakes.wrong: Using SMTP to receive mail.
mistakes.right: SMTP sends mail. POP3 and IMAP receive it.

subtopics.notes:
### Ports, numbered doors on a machine
The IP address finds the computer. The **port number** finds the service on it. Learn this classic set.

| Protocol | Port | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **HTTP** | **80** | web pages (plain) |
| **HTTPS** | **443** | web pages, encrypted with TLS/SSL |
| **FTP** | **21** (control), 20 (data) | file transfer |
| **SSH** | **22** | secure remote login |
| **Telnet** | **23** | remote login, not encrypted |
| **SMTP** | **25** | sending e-mail |
| **DNS** | **53** | name to IP resolution |
| **DHCP** | 67 / 68 | automatic IP assignment |
| **POP3** | **110** | receiving e-mail (download) |
| **IMAP** | **143** | receiving e-mail (sync) |
| **SNMP** | 161 | network management |
| **RDP** | 3389 | Windows remote desktop |

> **Tip:** 21, 22, 23 climb in order: FTP, SSH, Telnet. Then 25 is SMTP. 80 and 443 are the web pair. 110 and 143 bring mail in.

### TCP vs UDP
| | **TCP** | **UDP** |
|---|---|---|
| Full form | Transmission Control Protocol | User Datagram Protocol |
| Connection | connection-oriented (handshake first) | connectionless (just send) |
| Delivery | guaranteed and ordered | no guarantee |
| Speed | slower | faster, low overhead |
| Used by | web, e-mail, file transfer | DNS queries, DHCP, streaming, VoIP, gaming |

The TCP handshake has three steps: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

> **Example:** Live cricket streaming uses UDP. One lost frame is better than a paused match.

### One web visit, step by step
1. **DNS** turns the name into an IP address.
2. **TCP** opens the connection.
3. **HTTPS** (port 443) asks for the page and delivers it encrypted.

For e-mail, SMTP sends. POP3 or IMAP receive.

### Reading a protocol question
Decide what the question asks. Then use the matching tool.

- **Direction:** send mail is SMTP. Receive mail is POP3 or IMAP.
- **Number:** recall the port anchors. If unsure, eliminate by neighbourhood.
- **Style:** reliable means TCP. Fast means UDP.
- **Full form:** spell it out from the name.

> **Tip:** For TCP or UDP, ask what a lost packet costs. A corrupted file is bad, so use TCP. One blurred video frame is fine, so use UDP.

### Full forms to memorise
- HTTP: HyperText Transfer Protocol. HTTPS: secure HTTP over TLS/SSL.
- FTP: File Transfer Protocol. SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol.
- POP: Post Office Protocol. IMAP: Internet Message Access Protocol.
- DNS: Domain Name System. DHCP: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. SSH: Secure Shell.

> **Watch:** Telnet sends everything in plain text. SSH (22) is the encrypted replacement.

patterns.name: Port-number matching
patterns.howToSpot: HTTPS works on which port, the port of SMTP, FTP, DNS or POP3, or a matched pair with one number shifted.
steps: Recall the anchors: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, POP3 110, IMAP 143.
Watch for 443 given to HTTP or 80 given to HTTPS.
Use the climbing run 21, 22, 23.
Eliminate by neighbourhood if unsure.
patterns.why: Port numbers are fixed facts, so anchors beat guessing.

example.q: HTTPS uses which port number by default?
steps: HTTPS is secure web traffic.
The port is 443. Plain HTTP uses 80.

patterns.name: TCP vs UDP selection
patterns.howToSpot: Which protocol is used for live streaming or file transfer, which is connection-oriented, or reliability-versus-speed statements.
steps: Ask what a lost packet would cost.
A corrupted file is costly: TCP.
One blurred frame is fine: UDP.
Live streaming, gaming, VoIP, DNS queries: UDP.
patterns.why: Reliability needs TCP. Speed needs UDP.

example.q: Which transport protocol suits a live cricket stream?
steps: Speed matters more than perfect delivery.
TCP retransmission would only pause the match.

patterns.name: Protocol purpose identification
patterns.howToSpot: Which protocol transfers files, sends e-mail or resolves names. It is purpose matching.
steps: File transfer: FTP. Send mail: SMTP.
Receive mail: POP3 or IMAP. Web pages: HTTP or HTTPS.
Names to IPs: DNS. Remote login: Telnet (plain) or SSH (secure).
DHCP assigns IP addresses.
patterns.why: Each protocol was built for one purpose.

example.q: Which protocol is used to transfer files between computers?
steps: File transfer is the purpose.
FTP uses port 21 for control and 20 for data.

patterns.name: Protocol full forms and security
patterns.howToSpot: Full form of FTP, TCP, UDP or DHCP, which remote-login protocol is secure, or Telnet-versus-SSH statements.
steps: Spell out the full form from the name.
Telnet (23) sends plain text.
SSH (22) is the encrypted replacement.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS/SSL.
patterns.why: The S in SSH and HTTPS means secure.

example.q: Which protocol provides an encrypted remote login?
steps: Telnet on port 23 sends passwords as plain text.
SSH is the encrypted one.

patterns.name: Mail protocol direction
patterns.howToSpot: Which protocol sends mail, which downloads it, or which keeps mail in sync across devices.
steps: Sending: SMTP (port 25).
Downloading: POP3 (port 110).
Syncing: IMAP (port 143).
All three run over TCP.
patterns.why: Sending and receiving use different protocols.

example.q: Which protocol is used to send e-mail?
steps: Sending is the direction asked.
SMTP is the sender; POP3 and IMAP receive.

patterns.name: Less common ports and services
patterns.howToSpot: Ports 67/68, 161 or 3389, or which service uses them.
steps: DHCP uses 67 and 68.
SNMP (network management) uses 161.
RDP (Windows remote desktop) uses 3389.
FTP data port is 20.
patterns.why: These ports appear less often but are fixed facts.

example.q: Windows Remote Desktop uses which port?
steps: RDP means Remote Desktop Protocol.
Its port is 3389.

revision: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, POP3 110, IMAP 143.
TCP is reliable and connection-oriented (web, mail, FTP). UDP is fast and connectionless (streaming, games, VoIP).
Telnet is plain text. SSH (22) is its encrypted replacement.
HTTPS is HTTP plus TLS/SSL encryption.
SMTP sends mail. POP3 and IMAP receive mail.
DNS resolves names to IP addresses. DHCP assigns IP addresses.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which device sends data to all ports', 'which device connects two different networks', 'which device regenerates a weak signal' — a behaviour is described and the device named.
pyqPatterns.approach: Climb the ladder: hub = broadcasts to every port (Layer 1); switch = learns MAC addresses, sends only to the right port (Layer 2); router = joins different networks and routes by IP (Layer 3); repeater = regenerates signals; modem = modulator-demodulator; gateway = protocol converter. Match the verb in the question to the one-line job.

example.q: Which device forwards a data packet towards the correct network using IP addresses?
example.solution: Router — it works on Layer 3, reading IP addresses and choosing the best path between networks.

pyqPatterns.pattern: OSI layer count, order and functions
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many layers in the OSI model', 'routing/encryption/framing is a ___ layer function', 'a router/switch works at which layer', correct-order statements.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the map: 7 layers — Physical (bits), Data Link (frames, MAC), Network (IP, routing), Transport (TCP/UDP, ports), Session (dialogues), Presentation (translation, encryption, compression), Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP). Devices: hub 1, switch 2, router 3. The planted traps: encryption at Application, routing at Transport.

example.q: In the OSI model, routing of packets is the function of which layer?
example.solution: Network (Layer 3) — IP addressing and route selection; Transport (4) only delivers end to end.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: An address is printed (10.0.0.5, 130.10.5.2, 196.1.2.3, 225.1.1.1) and its class asked; or the first-octet range of a class; or 'which is a private address'; 'what is 127.0.0.1'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the FIRST octet only against the ruler 1(A) - 128(B) - 192(C) - 224(D) - 240(E); 127 = loopback. Private ranges: 10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x. Multicast = Class D. One octet decides everything — do not read the second number.

example.q: The IP address 130.10.5.2 belongs to which class?
example.solution: Class B — the first octet 130 lies between 128 and 191.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'HTTPS works on which port', 'SMTP port', 'FTP uses which ports', or a matched pair where one number is shifted.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchors: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21 (data 20), SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, POP3 110, IMAP 143. The classic trap swaps 80 and 443, or pairs POP3 with 143 (that is IMAP). Climb 21-22-23 for FTP-SSH-Telnet.

example.q: Data transfer of the World Wide Web over an encrypted connection uses which default port?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which protocol for live streaming / file download', 'which is connection-oriented', statements about reliability and speed.
pyqPatterns.approach: TCP = connection-oriented, reliable, ordered — web pages, e-mail, file transfer. UDP = connectionless, fast, no guarantee — live streaming, gaming, VoIP, DNS queries. The recurring answer: live video = UDP; downloading a file = TCP.

example.q: Which protocol would a live video streaming service prefer?
example.solution: UDP — speed matters more than perfect delivery; TCP's retransmissions would only pause the stream.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Every computer connected to a central hub', 'every node connected to every other node', 'all computers share a single backbone' — the layout described and the topology asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Central device with all nodes = Star; every node to every other = Mesh; one shared backbone with terminators = Bus; circle of neighbours = Ring; stars joined on a backbone = Tree. Also know failure points: star dies with its hub, bus dies with its backbone, mesh is the most reliable.

example.q: In which topology does every node have a direct link to every other node?
example.solution: Mesh — the most reliable topology, needing n(n-1)/2 links.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many links are required for a mesh of 5/6/8 computers' — pure arithmetic.
pyqPatterns.approach: links = n x (n-1) / 2. For n = 4 give 6; n = 5 give 10; n = 6 give 15; n = 8 give 28. The trap option is n squared or the unhalved n(n-1).

example.q: How many cable links are needed for a full mesh of 6 computers?

solvedExamples.q: A fully connected mesh network is made with 6 computers. How many duplex links are required?
solvedExamples.solution: Full mesh links = n(n-1)/2 = 6x5/2 = 15. (n(n-1) = 30 counts every link twice, once from each end.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Apply n(n-1)/2 directly; the 30 option is the 'forgot to halve' trap.

solvedExamples.q: Which device connects two different networks and routes packets between them using IP addresses?
solvedExamples.solution: A router works at the Network layer, reading IP addresses to forward packets between distinct networks (e.g. your LAN to the Internet). Hubs broadcast at the physical layer, switches forward frames by MAC within one LAN, repeaters only regenerate signals.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 'Two DIFFERENT networks + IP' = router, every time.

solvedExamples.q: Match the OSI layer with its function: (a) Transport (b) Data Link (c) Presentation - (i) MAC addressing and framing (ii) encryption and compression (iii) end-to-end delivery using ports
solvedExamples.solution: Transport (layer 4) gives end-to-end delivery with port numbers (a-iii). Data Link (2) frames data and uses MAC addresses (b-i). Presentation (6) handles format, encryption and compression (c-ii).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Port = Transport, MAC/frame = Data Link, encrypt = Presentation - three clean anchors.

solvedExamples.q: The IP addresses 10.0.0.5, 172.20.1.9 and 192.168.0.10 belong respectively to which classes?
solvedExamples.solution: First octets: 10 falls in 1-126 (Class A), 172 in 128-191 (Class B), 192 in 192-223 (Class C). All three are also private-range addresses.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Apply the ruler to the first octet only; ignore the rest of the address.

practice.q: A network confined to a single office building is classified as a:
practice.solution: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a room, building or campus. MANs span cities, WANs span countries/continents.
practice.shortcut: Local = LAN; City = MAN; Wide/world = WAN.

practice.q: In which topology is every node connected to every other node by a dedicated link?
practice.solution: Full mesh gives each pair of nodes its own direct link - maximum reliability at maximum cable cost (n(n-1)/2 links).

practice.q: Which network device broadcasts received data to all connected ports without any addressing intelligence?
practice.solution: A hub is a multi-port repeater - it blindly repeats every bit to every port. Switches consult a MAC table; routers consult IP routes.
practice.shortcut: Dumb broadcast = hub; smart selection = switch.

practice.q: The number of layers in the OSI reference model is:
practice.solution: OSI has 7 layers (Application to Physical). The TCP/IP model that the Internet actually uses has 4.

practice.q: At which layer of the OSI model does a switch primarily operate?
practice.solution: Switches forward frames using MAC (hardware) addresses, which belong to the Data Link layer (2). Routers use IP at layer 3.
practice.shortcut: MAC-address device = layer 2; IP device = layer 3.

practice.q: Encryption and data compression in the OSI model are the responsibility of the:
practice.solution: Presentation (layer 6) translates data formats and applies encryption/compression (JPEG, MP3, TLS concepts). Session manages dialogues, Transport moves segments.

practice.q: How many links are needed for a full mesh topology with 5 computers?
practice.shortcut: Five nodes -> 5x4/2; the 20 option is the un-halved trap for those using n(n-1) with n=5... actually 20 = n x (n-1), another halving slip - always divide by 2.

practice.q: The IP address 127.0.0.1 is used for:
options: Loopback testing of the local machine
practice.solution: 127.x.x.x (typically 127.0.0.1 = localhost) loops packets back to the sender's own TCP/IP stack for self-testing.

practice.q: An IPv4 address is how many bits long?
practice.solution: IPv4 = 32 bits (four octets). IPv6 expanded this to 128 bits written in hexadecimal.

practice.q: Which of the following is a private IP address commonly used by home routers?
practice.solution: 192.168.0.0/16 is reserved for private networks - the default address of most home routers. 172.32 lies outside the private 172.16-172.31 block, 169.254.x.x is APIPA/link-local, and 8.8.8.8 is Google's public DNS.
practice.shortcut: The private trio: 10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x. Everything else is public.

practice.q: The default port number for HTTPS traffic is:
practice.solution: HTTPS runs over TLS on port 443; 80 is plain HTTP, 21 is FTP control, 8080 is a common alternate proxy port.

practice.q: Which protocol is normally used by live audio/video streaming where speed matters more than perfect delivery?
practice.solution: UDP is connectionless with no retransmission overhead, so realtime media, VoIP and gaming prefer it. TCP guarantees ordered delivery (web, mail, downloads).

practice.q: A modem's function is to:
options: Convert digital signals to analog and back
practice.solution: MOdulator-DEModulator: it turns the computer's digital bits into analog carrier tones (and vice versa) for transmission over telephone/cable plant. Routing is a router; rule-filtering is a firewall.
practice.shortcut: Digital <-> analog conversion is the modem's whole identity.

practice.q: The Wi-Fi wireless LAN standard family is designated by IEEE:
practice.solution: IEEE 802.11 covers Wi-Fi (a/b/g/n/ac/ax). 802.3 is wired Ethernet, 802.15 Bluetooth/PAN, 802.16 WiMAX.

practice.q: In a star topology, failure of the central hub/switch:
options: Has no effect on other nodes
Brings down communication between all nodes
Affects only the node next to the hub
Converts the network to a ring
practice.solution: Every node's cable meets at the central device, so its failure isolates the entire network - star's well-known single point of failure (individual cable breaks, however, affect only one node).
practice.shortcut: Centre dies, star dies - that weakness is the exam favourite.

practice.q: A network limited to a single building or campus is a —
practice.solution: **LAN = Local Area Network** — one building or campus, privately owned, fast.

practice.q: The Internet is the largest example of a —
practice.solution: **WAN = Wide Area Network** spanning countries and continents — the Internet is the biggest WAN.

practice.q: A Bluetooth connection between a phone and a wireless earphone is a —
practice.solution: **PAN = Personal Area Network** — about 10 metres around one person.

practice.q: Arrange by increasing span: 1. MAN 2. PAN 3. WAN 4. LAN
practice.solution: PAN (person) < LAN (building) < MAN (city) < WAN (world).

practice.q: Which topology connects every node to a central hub or switch?
practice.solution: **Star topology** — all nodes hang off one central device.

practice.q: In which topology does every node have a dedicated link to EVERY other node?
practice.solution: **Mesh** = all-to-all links — maximum reliability, maximum cable.

practice.q: A network where all computers share ONE common backbone cable uses —
practice.solution: **Bus topology** taps every node into one backbone with terminators at both ends.

practice.q: Which topology joins several star networks onto a single backbone?
practice.solution: **Tree (hierarchical)** = star networks connected by a bus backbone — scalable for large campuses.
practice.shortcut: Tree = stars on a branch line.

practice.q: How many links are required for a full mesh of 6 computers?
practice.solution: n(n-1)/2 = 6x5/2 = **15 links**. 30 forgets the halving; 36 is n squared.

practice.q: A full mesh of 8 computers needs how many links?
practice.solution: 8x7/2 = **28**. 56 skips the halving; 64 is 8 squared.

practice.q: Adding a 5th computer to a full mesh of 4 requires how many NEW links?
practice.solution: Mesh of 4 has 6 links, of 5 has 10 — the new computer connects to each existing node: **4 new links**.
practice.shortcut: New node joins every old node.

practice.q: Which topology has a SINGLE POINT of total failure at its central device?
practice.solution: If the **central hub/switch dies in a star, the whole network dies** — its one weakness.

practice.q: Which topology is the MOST reliable but also the most expensive to cable?
practice.solution: **Mesh** — every node has many alternate paths, so no single cut disconnects anyone; the price is n(n-1)/2 cables.

practice.q: In a bus topology, what happens if the main backbone cable is cut?
practice.solution: The backbone IS the bus — a cut splits it and no node can reach another (that is why terminators and cable quality matter).

practice.q: Wired Ethernet is standardised as IEEE —
practice.solution: **802.3 = Ethernet (wired LAN)**; 802.11 = Wi-Fi; 802.15 = Bluetooth.

practice.q: Which pair is wrongly matched?
practice.solution: Wi-Fi is **802.11**; 802.3 is the wired Ethernet standard — the planted swap.

practice.q: Which network device broadcasts incoming data to ALL its ports?
practice.solution: A **hub shouts to everyone**; it cannot read addresses (Layer 1 only).

practice.q: Which device reads MAC addresses and sends frames only to the correct port?
practice.solution: **Switch (Layer 2)** learns which MAC lives on which port — no wasted broadcasting.

practice.q: Which device connects two DIFFERENT networks and selects the best path for packets?
practice.solution: **Router (Layer 3)** works on IP addresses and chooses routes between networks.

practice.q: Your home Wi-Fi router joins your family's devices to the Internet. In networking terms it is acting as a —
options: Router connecting a LAN to a WAN
practice.solution: The home box routes between your **LAN** and the ISP's network (**WAN/Internet**), besides serving Wi-Fi.

practice.q: A modem is a short form of —
practice.solution: **MOdulator-DEModulator** — converts the computer's digital signals to the phone line's analog form and back.

practice.q: Which device regenerates a weak signal to extend the length of a network run?
practice.solution: **Repeater (Layer 1)** rebuilds the clean signal so it can travel farther.

practice.q: A gateway differs from a router mainly because it —
practice.solution: A **gateway is a protocol converter** — the entry/exit door between different worlds; a router only selects routes.

practice.q: Which device joins TWO LAN segments and filters traffic between them at Layer 2?
practice.solution: **Bridge (Layer 2)** connects two segments and holds local traffic back — an ancestor of the switch.

practice.q: A hub operates at which OSI layer?
practice.solution: A hub only repeats electrical signals — **Layer 1**, no addressing at all.

practice.q: A switch operates at which OSI layer?
practice.solution: **Layer 2** — switches read MAC addresses inside frames.

practice.q: Which sequence of devices is in ASCENDING order of intelligence?
practice.solution: Hub (no brain, L1) < Switch (MAC, L2) < Router (IP routing, L3).

practice.q: A MAC address is a —
options: 48-bit physical address fixed by the manufacturer
practice.solution: **MAC = 48 bits, burnt into the NIC**; 32-bit logical describes an IPv4 address.

practice.q: Which address CHANGES when a laptop moves from your home network to office Wi-Fi?
practice.solution: The **IP is logical and network-dependent**; the MAC stays burnt into the card forever.

practice.q: The OSI reference model has how many layers?
practice.solution: **OSI = 7 layers**; the TCP/IP model has 4.

practice.q: Which is the correct order of OSI layers from BOTTOM to TOP?
options: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Physical, Network, Data Link, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
Data Link, Physical, Transport, Network, Session, Presentation, Application
practice.solution: Bottom-up: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way.
practice.shortcut: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

practice.q: Which OSI layer sits DIRECTLY above the Transport layer?
practice.solution: Order above Transport: **Session (5), Presentation (6), Application (7)**.

practice.q: Routing of packets is the job of which OSI layer?
practice.solution: **Network (Layer 3)** handles IP addressing and routing.

practice.q: Framing and MAC addressing are functions of the —
practice.solution: **Data Link (Layer 2)** wraps bits into frames and uses MAC addresses; switches live here.

practice.q: Encryption and compression of data are handled by the —
practice.solution: **Presentation (Layer 6)** = translation, encryption, compression — the format preparer.

practice.q: Which statement about the Transport layer is TRUE?
options: It provides end-to-end delivery using ports (TCP/UDP)
practice.solution: Transport (4) = segmentation, ports, TCP/UDP. Routing is Layer 3, encryption Layer 6, signals Layer 1.

practice.q: At which OSI layer does a ROUTER work?
practice.solution: Routers read IP addresses and route — **Layer 3**.

practice.q: HTTP, FTP and SMTP belong to which OSI layer?
practice.solution: User-facing services sit on **Layer 7 (Application)**.

practice.q: IP as a protocol operates at the —
practice.solution: **IP = Internet Protocol, Layer 3** — addressing and routing; TCP/UDP sit above it on Layer 4.

practice.q: The TCP/IP model has how many layers?
practice.solution: **TCP/IP = 4 layers**: Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.

practice.q: Which OSI layers are merged into the Application layer of the TCP/IP model?
practice.solution: TCP/IP's **Application swallows OSI 5+6+7**; its Network Access layer takes 1+2.

practice.q: The IP address 130.10.5.2 belongs to which class?
practice.solution: First octet 130 lies in **128-191 = Class B**.

practice.q: Which class does the address 196.20.5.1 belong to?
practice.solution: First octet 196 is in **192-223 = Class C** — the small-network class.

practice.q: Class D IP addresses are used for —
practice.solution: **Class D (224-239) = multicast groups**; Class E (240-255) is experimental.

practice.q: The first octet of a Class A address runs from —
practice.solution: Class A = **1-126**; the 127 block is reserved for loopback, not ordinary Class A use.

practice.q: The address 127.0.0.1 refers to —
practice.solution: **127.0.0.1 = localhost** — a machine talking to itself for testing.

practice.q: Which of these is a PRIVATE IP address?
practice.solution: Private ranges: **10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x**. Note 172.32 is outside 16-31, hence public.

practice.q: The typical default address typed to open a home router's settings page is —
practice.solution: Home routers commonly sit at **192.168.1.1** — a private Class C address.

practice.q: An IPv4 address is how many bits long?
practice.solution: **IPv4 = 32 bits** — four octets of 8 bits each.

practice.q: An IPv6 address is written as —
options: Eight hexadecimal groups separated by colons
Four decimal numbers separated by dots
Six binary groups separated by dashes
practice.solution: **IPv6 = 128 bits in 8 hex groups with colons**, e.g. 2001:0db8::7334; IPv4 is dotted decimal.

practice.q: IPv6 was developed mainly because —
practice.solution: 32 bits give about **4.3 billion addresses** — too few for the connected world; 128 bits give a practically endless supply.

practice.q: Which statement about MAC and IP addresses is TRUE?
options: MAC is logical; IP is burnt into the NIC
Both are burnt into the NIC
MAC is physical and fixed; IP is logical and assignable
practice.solution: **MAC = 48-bit hardware identity; IP = software-assigned logical address** that changes with the network.

practice.q: A Class C network provides how many USABLE host addresses?
practice.solution: 256 total minus the **network address** and the **broadcast address** = **254 usable**.

practice.q: A device address reads 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E with colons and hexadecimal pairs. This is a —
practice.solution: Six hexadecimal pairs = **48-bit MAC** (IPv6 would show eight groups; IPv4 four decimal numbers).

practice.q: HTTPS uses which default port?
practice.solution: **HTTPS = 443**; plain HTTP uses 80.

practice.q: SMTP sends mail through port —
practice.solution: **SMTP = 25**; POP3 receives on 110 and IMAP on 143.

practice.q: Which pair of ports belongs to FTP?
practice.solution: **FTP: 21 = control commands, 20 = data** — the two-channel protocol.

practice.q: Match: 1. DNS 2. Telnet 3. POP3 — a. 23 b. 110 c. 53
practice.solution: DNS = 53, Telnet = 23, POP3 = 110.

practice.q: Which transport protocol is CONNECTION-ORIENTED and reliable?
practice.solution: **TCP** opens a connection, numbers segments and retransmits losses — reliable delivery.

practice.q: Live video streaming and online gaming normally use —
practice.solution: **UDP** is fast and never pauses to retransmit — one lost frame beats a frozen picture.

practice.q: Downloading a large software file from the Internet should use —
practice.solution: A file must arrive complete and in order — **TCP's reliability** is worth its slowness.

practice.q: Which service typically runs its queries over UDP?
practice.solution: A single quick query-and-reply fits **UDP** (port 53); mail, FTP and HTTPS ride on reliable TCP.

practice.q: Which protocol is used to transfer files between computers over a network?
practice.solution: **FTP = File Transfer Protocol** — control on port 21, data on 20.

practice.q: Which service automatically assigns IP addresses to devices joining a network?
practice.solution: **DHCP = Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol** — hands each device its IP settings.

practice.q: HTTPS differs from HTTP because it —
options: Uses a different type of cable
practice.solution: HTTPS = **HTTP inside an encrypted TLS/SSL tunnel** (port 443) — same web, locked line.

practice.q: Which remote-login protocol sends data, including passwords, WITHOUT encryption?
practice.solution: **Telnet (23) is plaintext** — SSH (22) is its encrypted modern replacement.

practice.q: UDP stands for —
practice.solution: **UDP = User Datagram Protocol** — connectionless, no delivery guarantee, very fast.
